assumptions: GWAS with possible polygenic signal and confounding
conclusion: Existing approaches cannot distinguish inflation due to true polygenic signal from confounding bias.
span: Both polygenicity (i.e., many small genetic effects) and confounding biases, such as cryptic relatedness and population stratification, can yield an inflated distribution of test statistics in genome-wide association studies (GWAS). However, current methods cannot distinguish between inflation from true polygenic signal and bias.

assumptions: Polygenic model with independently drawn effect sizes and the stated frequency-dependent variance
conclusion: The polygenic model draws effect sizes independently from distributions whose variance depends on allele frequency as specified in the model.
scope: Effect-size model underlying Equation (1); this sentence specifies a distributional variance structure rather than a fitted penalty.
span: Under a polygenic model, such that effect sizes are drawn independently from distributions with variance proportional to p(1-p)−1/2 where p is minor allele frequency (MAF),

objects: E[chi-square_j | LD Score_j]; N; h2; M; a; LD Score_j
assumptions: Polygenic effect-size model described immediately before Equation (1)
conclusion: Expected association chi-square is N*h2*LD Score/M + N*a + 1, and the stated relationship also holds for meta-analysis and ascertained binary traits with observed-scale h2.
scope: Conditional mean model, not a complete likelihood; binary-trait heritability is on the observed scale.
span: Under a polygenic model, such that effect sizes are drawn independently from distributions with variance proportional to p(1-p)−1/2 where p is minor allele frequency (MAF), then the expected χ2-statistic of variant j is E [ χ^{2} | ℓ_{j} ] = N h^{2} ℓ_{j} / M + N a + 1 , (1) where N is sample size; M is the number of SNPs, such that h2/M is the average heritability explained per SNP; a measures the contribution of confounding biases, such as cryptic relatedness and population stratification; and ℓ_{j} ≔ Σ_{k} r_{j k}^{2} is the LD Score of variant j, which measures the amount of genetic variation tagged by j and (a full derivation of this equation is provided in the Supplementary Note). This relationship holds for meta-analyses, and also for ascertained studies of binary phenotypes, in which case h2 is on the observed scale.

objects: LD Score regression intercept; confounding inflation
conclusion: Regressing GWAS chi-square statistics on LD Score yields an intercept minus one that estimates the mean contribution of confounding bias to inflation.
scope: Model-conditional estimation statement, not a finite-sample calibration theorem.
span: Consequently, if we regress χ2statistics from GWAS against LD Score (LD Score regression), the intercept minus one is an estimator of the mean contribution of confounding bias to the inflation in the test statistics.

objects: Reference-panel genotypes; estimated pairwise r2; LD Score
assumptions: Reference panel chosen for the GWAS population
conclusion: LD Scores are estimated from reference-panel genotypes using an unbiased r2 estimator summed within a genetic-distance window.
scope: The reported implementation uses European 1000 Genomes samples, 1 cM windows, excludes singletons and applies no r2 cutoff.
span: We estimated LD Scores from the European ancestry samples in the 1000 Genomes Project7 (EUR) using an unbiased estimator8 of r2 with 1 centiMorgan (cM) windows, singletons excluded (MAF > 0.13%) and no r2 cutoff.

objects: Weighted regression; LD Score restricted to regression SNPs; covariance of chi-square statistics
assumptions: Population LD consists of blocks and every r2 is zero or one for exact equivalence
conclusion: Reciprocal LD Score weighting approximates GLS for correlated chi-square statistics and is equivalent to GLS under the stated zero-or-one block-LD condition.
scope: The full covariance matrix is intractable; the equivalence is restricted to the stated idealized LD structure.
span: As an approximation, we correct for correlation by weighting variant j by the reciprocal of the LD Score of variant j counting LD only with other SNPs included in the regression. Precisely, if we let S denote the set of variants included in the LD Score regression then the LD Score of variant j counting LD only with other SNPs included in the regression is ℓ_{j} ( S ) ≔ 1 + ∑_{k ∈ S} r_{j k}^{2} Weighting by 1/lj(S) would be equivalent to GLS with the full variance-covariance matrix of χ2-statistics if the genome consisted of LD blocks and r2 (in the population) was either zero or one.

objects: Conditional variance of chi-square; normalized genotype effects; regression weights
assumptions: Additional normality assumption for per-normalized-genotype effect sizes
conclusion: Reciprocal conditional-variance weighting addresses heteroskedasticity under normally distributed normalized effects; violating normality increases standard error without biasing the regression.
scope: Normality is needed for the stated variance-weight formula, rather than for unbiasedness of regression.
span: To account for heteroskedasticity, we weight by 1 ( 1 + N h_{g}^{2} ℓ_{j} / M )^{2}, which is the reciprocal of the conditional variance function Var [ χ_{j}^{2} | ℓ_{j} ] under our model if we make the additional assumption that per-normalized genotype effect sizes are normally distributed (note that violation of this assumption does not bias the regression, it only increases the standard error. A derivation is provided in the Supplementary Note).

objects: LD Score measurement error; regression slope; jackknife standard errors
conclusion: Jackknife LD Score standard errors are used to correct attenuation bias in the fitted regression slope.
scope: Finite-reference measurement-error correction described in the overview; no independent validation of the correction formula is inferred.
span: Standard errors were estimated by jackknifing over blocks of individuals, and we used these standard errors to correct for attenuation bias in LD Score regression (i.e., the downward bias in the magnitude of the regression slope that results when the regressor is measured noisily, see Online Methods).

assumptions: No systematic correlation between FST and LD Score
conclusion: The model assumes no systematic FST-LD Score correlation; positive correlation would make the intercept underestimate population-stratification inflation.
scope: Linked selection can violate this assumption.
span: The model assumes that that there is no systematic correlation between FST and LD Score (see Supplementary Note). This assumption may be violated in practice as a result of linked selection (i.e., positive selection10 and background selection11). If there were a positive correlation between LD Score and FST , the LD Score regression intercept would underestimate the contribution of population stratification to the inflation in χ2statistics.

objects: Reference and target LD Scores; regression slope; intercept
assumptions: Reference LD differs from GWAS-population LD through mean-zero noise or systematic shifts
conclusion: Systematically higher or lower reference-population LD Scores bias the regression intercept downward or upward respectively.
scope: Reference-panel matching matters beyond ordinary LD Score sampling error.
span: Secondly and perhaps more importantly, consider the scenario where there is a directional bias in average LD Score such that the LD Scores in the reference population are systematically higher or lower than in the target population. Under such a scenario, then the LD Score regression intercept will be biased downwards or upwards, respectively (Online Methods).
location: buliksullivan2015 | PMC author manuscript | RESULTS > Overview of Methods

objects: Variance explained per SNP; LD Score; MAF
assumptions: Variance explained per SNP may correlate with LD Score
conclusion: Correlation between per-SNP variance explained and LD Score is a limitation; the selectively neutral example predicts downward intercept bias and upward slope bias.
scope: Optimal behavior is stated when variance explained per SNP is uncorrelated with LD Score.
span: A potential limitation of LD Score regression is that variance explained per SNP may be correlated with LD Score for some phenotypes. For an example where this might occur, consider a phenotype that is selectively neutral, so that per-allele effect size is uncorrelated with MAF (which means that variance explained is positively correlated with MAF, as additive genetic variance is defined as 2pqa2 where p and q are the major and minor allele frequency and a is the additive genetic effect). Since LD Score is also positively correlated with MAF, in this case we would expect variance explained to be positively correlated with LD Score, which will introduce downward bias in the LD Score regression intercept and upward bias in the LD Score regression slope, leading to an underestimate of potential bias.
location: buliksullivan2015 | PMC author manuscript | RESULTS > Frequency-Dependent Genetic Architectures

objects: Rare causal variants; LD Score regression slope; intercept
assumptions: Extreme architecture in which all causal variants have MAF < 1%
conclusion: When all causal variants are rare, the authors report that LD Score regression often yields a negative slope and an intercept above the mean chi-square.
scope: Simulation-based failure example for an extreme architecture, not a universal threshold theorem.
span: Nevertheless, there exist extreme genetic architectures where LD Score regression is not effective: for instance if all causal variants are rare (MAF < 1%, which may be an appropriate model for a phenotype under extreme negative selection), then LD Score regression will often generate a negative slope, and the intercept will be exceed the mean χ2 (Supplementary Figure 7).
location: buliksullivan2015 | PMC author manuscript | RESULTS > Frequency-Dependent Genetic Architectures

objects: Regression slope; heritability of SNPs entering LD Score
assumptions: Strong assumptions about rare-variant effect sizes
conclusion: Rescaling the regression slope estimates heritability explained by the SNPs used to estimate LD Score only under strong rare-effect assumptions, whose relaxation for robust heritability estimation is left for research.
scope: The authors separately state that the intercept is robust to these assumptions; this does not establish general slope robustness.
span: Under strong assumptions about the effect sizes of rare variants, the slope of the LD Score regression can be re-scaled to be an estimate of the heritability explained by all SNPs used in the estimation of the LD Scores (Supplementary Table 1). Relaxing these assumptions in order to obtain a robust estimate of the heritability explained by all 1000 Genomes SNPs is a direction for further research; however, we note that the LD Score regression intercept is robust to these assumptions.
location: buliksullivan2015 | PMC author manuscript | RESULTS > Overview of Methods

objects: LD Score intercept; genomic-control inflation factor lambda_GC
assumptions: Only summary data are available or conservative correction is desired; polygenic architecture
conclusion: The authors propose the LD Score intercept as a more robust confounding-inflation correction than genomic control, whose inflation factor increases with sample size under polygenicity.
scope: Direct confounding correction with genotype data remains preferable; extension to admixed populations remains future research.
span: However, in the event that only summary data are available, or if a conservative correction is desired, we propose that the LD Score regression intercept provides a more robust quantification of the extent of inflation from confounding bias than λGC (or intergenic λGC, Supplementary Table 8). Since λGCincreases with sample size in the presence of polygenicity (even without confounding bias)3, the gain in power obtained by correcting test statistics with the LD Score regression intercept instead of λGC will become even more substantial for larger GWAS. Extending this method to non-European populations such as East Asians or West Africans is straightforward given appropriate reference panels, but extension to admixed populations is the subject of future research.

objects: Number of causal variants; estimator variance
assumptions: Few causal variants in the reported polygenic simulations
conclusion: With few causal variants, the authors report unbiased estimates but very large standard errors and state that the approach is best suited to polygenic traits.
scope: Simulation-supported precision limitation; not a finite-sample unbiasedness theorem.
span: We note that if there are few causal variants, the LD Score regression estimates are still unbiased, but the standard errors become very large, meaning that this approach is best suited to polygenic traits (Supplementary Figures 3–5).
